:::{#exm-answer-information}
#### Two polar questions about the same number
<!-- no-figure: the example compares two numbers, with nothing to plot -->

Let $X$ be as in @exm-question,
let $A$ be the [answer](#def-answer) to each of the two questions below in turn,
and use base-2 [logarithms](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-logarithm).

- **"Is $X \ge 32$?"**
  Each [possible answer](#def-possible-answer) has [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $32/64 = 1/2$,
  so its [surprisal](#def-surprisal) is $1$ [bit](#def-bit),
  and the [entropy](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-entropy) of the answer, its [expected](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-expectation) surprisal, is $1$ bit.
  By @thm-answer-information, the answer carries $\mutinfof{X}{A} = 1$ bit about $X$.
- **"Is $X = 0$?"**
  The possible answer "yes" has probability $1/64$ and the possible answer "no" has probability $63/64$,
  so the entropy of the answer is

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \entropyf{A}
  &= -\tfrac{1}{64} \log_2 \tfrac{1}{64} - \tfrac{63}{64} \log_2 \tfrac{63}{64} \\
  &\approx 0.094 + 0.022 \\
  &\approx 0.116 \text{ bits}.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  By @thm-answer-information, the answer carries about $0.116$ bits about $X$.

The reply "yes" to "Is $X = 0$?" is worth $6$ bits,
but it is rare,
so on average asking "Is $X = 0$?" gains far less than the $1$ bit from "Is $X \ge 32$?".

:::
